article.title: Victims of Sexual Abuse
article.author: Sejal Desai
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. Yes, children can become victims of sexual abuse through online gaming platforms. Offenders use in-game chat, voice features, and private messages to build trust with children and then push them toward sexual contact or explicit images. California is the most populous state in the country and one of the world’s largest economies. It is home to Silicon Valley and many of the world’s best-known technology and video game companies. Major game studios operate in both the San Francisco Bay Area and Southern California. With so many popular games built there, online safety is a growing concern for families across the state. When a child is harmed, some parents speak with a child sex abuse lawyer in California to learn how offenders and others can be held accountable. How Gaming Platforms Create Risk Many games let children talk with strangers in real time, which gives offenders direct access to young users. Common risk points include: Open text and voice chat with unknown players Private messaging and friend requests In-game gifts, currency, or rare items Offenders often move the child from the game to a less monitored messaging or video app, where contact is harder to spot. What Grooming Often Looks Like Grooming is gradual. An offender builds a close bond so the child feels special or indebted. Warning Signs in the Online Relationship Parents may notice patterns such as: An older “friend” who gives frequent gifts or game currency Requests to keep the friendship secret Requests for photos or video calls Changes in the Child’s Behavior A groomed child may become secretive about devices or upset when gaming is limited. Some show sudden mood changes, withdraw from family, or have new items they cannot explain. In some cases, offenders demand more images by threatening to share photos the child already sent. This crime is often called sextortion. What Federal Law Says Online child exploitation is a federal crime. Under 18 U.S.C. § 2422(b), it is illegal to use the internet to persuade or entice a minor into sexual activity, and the offense carries a mandatory minimum of 10 years in prison. Victims also have civil options. Under 18 U.S.C. § 2255, a person exploited as a minor can sue the offender for damages of at least $150,000 plus attorney’s fees. Can Gaming Companies Be Held Responsible? Platform liability is more complex. A federal law known as Section 230, found at 47 U.S.C. § 230, often protects online platforms from liability for content posted by users. Recent lawsuits against gaming and chat companies argue that unsafe product design, weak age checks, and poor safety tools contributed to harm. Courts are still deciding these claims . Steps to Take If You Suspect Abuse Acting quickly can stop the contact and protect evidence. These steps can help: Block the offender, but do not delete the account or messages. Record usernames, dates, and screenshots of chats that do not contain explicit images. Report the activity to NCMEC’s CyberTipline and local law enforcement. Report the user to the gaming platform. Connect your child with a counselor who works with abuse survivors. Never copy, save, or forward explicit images of a child, even as evidence. Police can collect them directly. Key Takeaways Children can be sexually abused through contact that begins on gaming platforms. Offenders often use chat, gifts, secrecy, and threats to exploit young players. 18 U.S.C. § 2422(b) makes online enticement of a minor a federal crime. Victims may seek civil damages under 18 U.S.C. § 2255. Section 230 can limit platform liability, but courts are testing design-based claims. Preserving evidence and reporting quickly help protect the child and the case.
